content: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. {{v:2}} He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.” {{v:3}} Jesus answered him, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.” {{v:4}} Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” {{v:5}} Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom. {{v:6}} That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. {{v:7}} Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must all be born anew.’ {{v:8}} The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” {{v:9}} Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?” {{v:10}} Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? {{v:11}} Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness. {{v:12}} If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? {{v:13}} No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. {{v:14}} As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, {{v:15}} that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. {{v:16}} For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. {{v:17}} For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. {{v:18}} He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God. {{v:19}} This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil. {{v:20}} For everyone who does evil hates the light and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed. {{v:21}} But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”

facets.text: Jesus tells Nicodemus that unless one is born anew he cannot see the Kingdom of God, insisting that entrance into God's reign requires more than natural birth or human learning. The regeneration in view is not a repetition of physical birth, as Nicodemus supposes, but a new origin of life given from above. This establishes that salvation begins not in human initiative but in a birth that comes from God.
facets.question: Why is a new birth necessary to enter the Kingdom of God?

facets.text: Christ specifies that this new birth is 'of water and Spirit,' joining the outward sign of water to the inward gift of the Holy Spirit. The Catholic tradition reads this as a direct reference to the sacrament of Baptism, in which water and the Spirit together effect regeneration. The sacramental sign is not merely symbolic but the appointed means through which the Spirit gives new life.
facets.question: What does being born of water and the Spirit mean for Baptism?

facets.text: Jesus distinguishes flesh from spirit: 'That which is born of the flesh is flesh; that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.' Natural human generation cannot of itself produce supernatural life, which belongs to a different order entirely. This teaches the necessity of grace, since fallen human nature cannot elevate itself to the divine life apart from the Spirit's work.
facets.question: Why can't human nature attain divine life on its own?

facets.text: The Spirit is compared to the wind, which 'blows where it wants' and whose origin and destination remain hidden. The sovereignty and freedom of the Spirit's action mean that regeneration is God's gracious initiative, mysterious and not subject to human control. Yet its effects are real and perceptible, just as the wind's sound is heard even when its source is unseen.
facets.question: How does the mysterious freedom of the Holy Spirit work in the soul?

facets.text: Jesus grounds his testimony in the fact that the Son of Man alone has descended from heaven and can speak of heavenly things. His authority to reveal the mysteries of God rests on his divine origin and his unique union with the Father. Nicodemus, though 'the teacher of Israel,' cannot grasp these truths without receiving the witness of the One who comes from above.
facets.question: What gives Jesus the authority to reveal heavenly realities?

facets.text: The lifting up of the bronze serpent by Moses in the wilderness is presented as a type of the crucified Christ: 'even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.' Just as those bitten looked upon the serpent and lived, so those who believe in the crucified and exalted Son receive eternal life. The 'lifting up' unites Christ's crucifixion and glorification in a single saving act.
facets.question: How does the bronze serpent Moses raised prefigure the crucifixion of Christ?

facets.text: 'For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son' reveals that the whole economy of salvation springs from the Father's love. The Incarnation and the gift of the Son are not a response to human merit but the free overflow of divine love toward a world that could not save itself. Eternal life is offered to whoever believes, showing the universal scope of God's saving will.
facets.question: What does John 3:16 reveal about the source and motive of salvation?

facets.text: Christ declares that God sent his Son not to judge the world but to save it, so that belief brings life while unbelief is already a self-inflicted condemnation. Judgment is not an arbitrary sentence imposed from outside but the consequence of refusing the light that has come. Those who reject the Son 'have been judged already' precisely because they will not believe in his name.
facets.question: Did Jesus come to condemn the world or to save it?

facets.text: The passage closes with the imagery of light and darkness: men love darkness because their deeds are evil and fear exposure, while those who do the truth come to the light. This frames the acceptance or rejection of Christ as a moral drama bound up with the orientation of one's works. Coming to the light means allowing one's deeds to be seen as 'done in God,' revealing that saving faith and moral integrity belong together.
facets.question: Why do people reject the light of Christ, and what does coming to the light mean?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Jesus' night discourse with Nicodemus on regeneration through water and the Spirit, the mystery of grace, the Son of Man lifted up as the crucified Savior, God's saving love for the world, and the judgment of light versus darkness.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: New birth from above is required to see God's Kingdom; salvation begins in God's initiative, not natural birth or human learning.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Being born of water and Spirit refers to Baptism, where the sacramental sign truly effects regeneration through the Holy Spirit.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Flesh cannot produce spirit; supernatural divine life requires grace because fallen nature cannot elevate itself.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The Spirit compared to wind shows the free, sovereign, hidden yet perceptible working of divine grace in regeneration.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Jesus' authority to reveal heavenly things rests on his divine origin as the Son of Man who descended from heaven.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The bronze serpent lifted by Moses prefigures the crucified and exalted Christ, whose lifting up unites cross and glory to give life to believers.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: John 3:16 reveals salvation as the free overflow of the Father's love, giving the Son for the life of all who believe.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The Son came to save, not condemn; unbelief is self-condemnation through rejection of the light.
[MORAL | explicit]: The light/darkness imagery links acceptance of Christ to the moral orientation of one's works; coming to the light joins faith and integrity.

content: After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. {{v:2}} He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. {{v:3}} Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him. {{v:4}} Peter answered and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” {{v:5}} While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” {{v:6}} When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. {{v:7}} Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” {{v:8}} Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone. {{v:9}} As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, “Don’t tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” {{v:10}} His disciples asked him, saying, “Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” {{v:11}} Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things; {{v:12}} but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.” {{v:13}} Then the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptizer.

facets.text: At the Transfiguration Jesus reveals the hidden glory of his divinity, letting his face shine like the sun and his garments become white as light. This is not a change imposed from outside but the radiance of what he always is, briefly disclosed to strengthen the disciples before the scandal of the Passion. The tradition sees here a foretaste of the glory of the risen Christ and of the beatitude promised to those united to him.
facets.question: What does the shining glory at the Transfiguration reveal about who Jesus is?

facets.text: The Father's voice from the bright cloud—'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.'—repeats the testimony given at the Baptism and adds a command to obey. The whole Trinity is present: the Father speaks, the Son is glorified, and the overshadowing cloud signals the Spirit. The words establish Jesus as the definitive Word to whom all must now listen, surpassing every earlier revelation.
facets.question: What does the Father's voice at the Transfiguration teach about listening to Jesus?

facets.text: Moses and Elijah appearing with Jesus present the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to him. Their conversation with Christ shows that all of the Old Testament points toward and finds its fulfillment in him, not as rivals to be housed in equal tents but as servants of the one Son. When the vision ends the disciples see 'no one, except Jesus alone,' underscoring that he alone is the fulfillment of what they represent.
facets.question: Why do Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus at the Transfiguration?

facets.text: Peter's desire to build three tents and to remain on the mountain expresses a genuine but premature longing to grasp glory apart from the cross. It is 'good to be here,' yet the disciples must descend and Jesus must suffer before the kingdom comes in fullness. The passage teaches that consolation in prayer is a gift to fortify the soul for the trials ahead, not a resting place to be clung to.
facets.question: What does Peter's wish to build three tents reveal about seeking God's glory without the cross?

facets.text: Jesus' command to tell no one 'until the Son of Man has risen from the dead' binds the Transfiguration to the Resurrection as its interpretive key. The glory glimpsed on the mountain can only be rightly understood in light of the empty tomb, so that the disciples are not to proclaim it until the Passion has given it its true meaning. Glory and suffering are inseparably joined in the mystery of Christ.
facets.question: Why did Jesus tell the disciples to keep the Transfiguration secret until after the Resurrection?

facets.text: In identifying John the Baptist as the Elijah who has already come, Jesus interprets the prophecy of Elijah's return as fulfilled in the forerunner who prepared his way. Yet John was not recognized and suffered at the hands of men, which Jesus makes a prophecy of his own coming Passion: 'Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.' The rejection of the messenger foreshadows the rejection of the Messiah.
facets.question: How is the prophecy of Elijah's return fulfilled in John the Baptist?

facets.text: The disciples fall on their faces in fear at the divine voice, and Jesus comes, touches them, and says, 'Get up, and don't be afraid.' The same Lord whose glory overwhelms them is the one who reaches out to raise and reassure them. This gesture reveals that the majesty of God draws near not to crush but to lift up the frightened human heart.
facets.question: How does Jesus respond to the disciples' fear before God's glory?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The Transfiguration discloses Christ's divine glory before three disciples, with Moses and Elijah as witnesses and the Father's voice commanding that the Son be heard; it binds glory to the Passion and identifies John the Baptist as the returning Elijah.

[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Christ's shining face and radiant garments reveal his hidden divinity and foreshadow the glory of his Resurrection and the beatitude of the blessed.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The Father's voice names Jesus his beloved Son and commands 'listen to him,' revealing the Trinity and establishing Christ as the definitive Word.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Moses and Elijah embody the Law and Prophets bearing witness to Christ, who alone remains as their fulfillment when the vision ends.
[MORAL | inferential]: Peter's wish to build tents and remain shows a premature grasping at glory apart from the cross; consolation in prayer fortifies the soul rather than becoming a resting place.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Jesus' command of silence until the Resurrection makes the empty tomb the key to the Transfiguration, joining glory and suffering inseparably.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who has come; John's rejection and suffering foreshadow the Passion of the Son of Man.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: Overwhelmed and afraid, the disciples are touched and raised by Jesus with 'don't be afraid,' showing that divine majesty draws near to lift up the human heart.
